questions.stem: Muckrakers of the period were careful to distinguish the merely {1} legislator, who pursued wealth as ardently as any speculator but broke no law in doing so, from his {2} colleague, whose committee vote could be had for a fixed and widely known sum.
questions.explanation: The sentence turns on a distinction between legal appetite and criminal sale, so blank one needs a pure greed word — acquisitive — and "broke no law in doing so" rules out venal there. Blank two must name what greed alone cannot: an office with a price list, which is venal. Avaricious and rapacious are also mere greed words, so choosing either would collapse the very contrast the sentence sets up.

questions.stem: Where his own students had merely admired the old philologist, the next generation came to {1} him, quoting his marginalia as though it were scripture and passing over his errors in embarrassed silence.
questions.explanation: Venerate and revere both name an attitude of deep, quasi-sacred respect that places its object above ordinary criticism, which is exactly what treating marginalia as scripture and errors as unmentionable amounts to. Canonize names a conferral of status by some authority rather than an attitude, lionize means to fête someone as a celebrity, and extol means to praise loudly — none of which fits a silence-keeping deference, and denigrate reverses the sense.

rejects.problem: "mercenary" is a genuine second answer. The sentence only establishes that the inspectors let money, not carelessness, drive them — money-motivated behavior — which "mercenary" names as well as "venal" does. "Venal" is the better fit because it carries the specific sense of a public official corruptible by bribes, matching the sale of a safety certificate at a known price, but nothing in the sentence rules out the broader "mercenary." Fix by removing "mercenary" or by adding a cue that the fee was illicit/off-the-books, which "mercenary" cannot cover.
rejects.stem: The port's building inspectors were not so much negligent as frankly {1}: a certificate of structural safety cost eighty dollars, and every contractor in the district knew the figure.

rejects.problem: Blank {2} is clean — "hunting out the seams in books long held sacred" forces "iconoclastic" ("deferential" reverses the contrast, "numinous" is a category error). Blank {1} is the defect: both "venerate" and "lionize" are defensible. The sentence only requires a verb meaning "praise uncritically / hold as beyond reproach," and lionize (to treat as an object of great celebrity/acclaim) satisfies that as well as venerate does; posthumous lionizing is standard usage, so "fifty years dead" does not rule it out. The intended discriminator is presumably that venerate pairs with "sacred"/"beyond reproach" while lionize targets a person's celebrity rather than the quality of individual chapters — too fine a distinction to mark a test-taker wrong on. Fix by replacing "lionize" with an option that is clearly unfit (e.g. "scrutinize" or "anthologize").
rejects.stem: Where an earlier generation of critics was content to {1} Melville — a writer fifty years dead and already installed in every syllabus — treating even his slackest chapters as beyond reproach, the present generation is aggressively {2}, hunting out the seams in books long held sacred.
